“Weirs are either straightforward or they kill you” – Franco Ferrero: Author Whitewater Safety & Rescue
This statement is born out by the facts – 41 fatalities from only the five largest weir accidents in Europe! Almost all multiple fatalities in rafting, kayaking and canoeing are due to weirs.
Accidents involving Weirs in Europe:
2008 – 5 soldiers drown rafting on the Kander river in Switzerland
2008 – 13 people drown in a weir while canoeing on the Sava river in Slovenia
1999 – 4 UK tourists drown commercially rafting on the Salzach river in Austria
1993 – 9 German tourists die rafting on the Inn river in Engadine, Switzerland
1975 – 10 soldiers drown at Cromwell Weir on the river Trent in England
Weirs are so dangerous because even with correct swiftwater rescue training and equipment, if the weir has sufficient towback, it will be almost impossible to self rescue from. Looking at these accidents we can class them into different accident types:
1. Ignorance of the danger
The accidents that occurred on the Kander, Sava and Inn rivers where all, to a large extent, caused by a ignorance of the danger posed by the weirs. Most weirs look very tame compared to sections of whitewater, and the amount of aerated water bears no relation to the amount of towback that will be present. Changes in water level can also account for changes in the amount of towback at a weir. This was the case on the Inn, where the group had successfully run the weir the day before, when less water was flowing.
Ignorance can also mean not knowing that there is a weir (or other deadly feature) on the section of river that you are paddling. In 2010 a party of 4 Russian rafters died in Norway when they put in on the wrong section of the Sjoa river, one where the whole river flows through a siphon.
if there is any doubt that a weir (or rapid) is dangerous, then it should always be portaged.
2. Missing the take out
The other two accidents were caused by the rafts missing the take out. On the Trent this was during a military night exercise, on the Salzach when a guest fell out of the raft during landing. This can also be a problem when unrunnable gorges or hard rapids are downstream. Always have everyone look at the take out when there is such a deadly hazard downstream, and get out a good distance above it.
It is far better to walk an extra 200m than miss the last eddy! During night exercises lights positioned to show the end of the exercise area are needed to prevent people continuing downstream and into other hazards.
People often find it difficult to assess the danger posed by a man made weir, unless they are very experienced in understanding swiftwater. The Environmental agency in Great Britain needed to assess the danger that weirs on rivers posed to the public. Take a look at this comprehensive weir assessment system that Rescue 3 UK developed to help them with this difficult task.
The system is divided up into 4 sections:
1. Weir hazard rating
2. Likelihood of weir to cause harm rating
3. Weir risk rating (1 x 2)
4. Weir rescue rating
The Weir Hazard rating looks at 10 structural factors of the weir such as – the amount of towback, depth of hydraulic, height of the drop, etc. Each factor is then rated with points from 0 to 5, and all the points added up for a total score.
Likelihood to cause harm tries to work out if anyone will be able to get stuck in the weir and looks at all the different ways that could happen. Again each factor gets a point score, which are added up for the overall rating.
The risk rating is produced by multiplying the hazard by the likelihood.
Lastly is the Rescue rating, it looks at 10 points that influence the ease of rescue such as – width of river, access on the banks, available anchors etc.
All in all it is a very good system especially for users who have very little experience of swiftwater rescue. Some people may find it’s mathematical nature a bit overly complex, as it takes a while to add all the points up. Others may ask why is there a need for likelihood and risk ratings. Don’t forget this system was developed mainly to prevent people from drowning in weirs and not just for rescue requirements.

Changes in water levels can also affect the amount of towback present. Accidents caused by missing the takeout have been observed during military night exercises and when guests fall out of rafts during landing. It's crucial to have everyone examine the takeout when there's a life-threatening obstacle downstream, and to ensure that everyone understands its location.

The Environmental Agency in Great Britain required assistance in assessing the danger that weirs pose to the general public. The weir hazard rating examines ten structural elements of the weir, including the magnitude of towback, the depth of the hydraulic, and the height of the drop, assigning scores ranging from 0 to 5 to each element. The likelihood of weir causing harm rating considers all the ways someone might become trapped in the weir. Each factor is assigned a score, which is summed to provide an overall rating. The risk rating is obtained by multiplying the hazard by the likelihood. Lastly, the rescue rating analyzes ten factors that impact the ease of rescue, such as the width of the river, bank accessibility, and available anchors. This system is particularly beneficial for individuals new to swiftwater rescue since it accounts for both rescue and prevention considerations. Introduction
The recent development of compact light sources in the terahertz band has led to the frontier research field of terahertz wave spectroscopy. A terahertz light source produced in an accelerator also serves as an excellent tool for evaluation of the accelerator. What is a paywall
A paywall is a way to restrict access to a website (most commonly publications) by soliciting a purchase or a subscription.

History

World War I
The 11th Division was first formed as a National Guard division in early 1917 consisting of units of the Michigan and Wisconsin National Guards. By the end of that same year, the 11th Division became the 32nd Division (later 32nd Infantry Division).

The 71st and 72nd Infantry Regiments were formed from cadres from the 17th and 63rd Regiments. The division's advanced schools detachment started for England on 25 October 1918, arriving 8 November 1918. With the Armistice, further activities were halted and the division disbanded on 29 November 1918 at Camp Meade, Maryland.

World War II (deception formation)

Screaming Life is the debut EP by the American rock band Soundgarden, released in October 1987 through Sub Pop Records. Screaming Life was later combined with the band's next EP, Fopp (1988), and released as the Screaming Life/Fopp compilation album in 1990.

Recording
The EP was recorded in 1987 in Seattle, Washington, at Reciprocal Studios with producer Jack Endino, who also produced albums for Nirvana and Mudhoney.

Music and lyrics
Drummer Matt Cameron described the sound on the EP as "pretty raw". "Hunted Down", Soundgarden's first single, is representative of the early "grunge" sound—with its dirty guitar, dissonant atmosphere and lyrics concerning entrapment and escape. "Nothing to Say" features drop D tuning, which would become a signature of Soundgarden's sound on later albums. Guitarist Kim Thayil said he learned about the tuning from Buzz Osborne of the Melvins, when Osborne was telling him about Black Sabbath.

Earlier versions of "Tears to Forget" appeared on the band's 1985 demo tape and on the 1986 Deep Six compilation album, which featured some of the first recordings by the earliest Seattle grunge bands, including Soundgarden. That version was recorded with drummer Scott Sundquist, but the version on Screaming Life was recorded with Cameron.

prompt: What is the difference between corporatism and socialism, and can a capitalist economy be considered corporatist or socialist?
response_a:
Corporatism and socialism are two distinct economic and political ideologies with significant differences.

Socialism is an economic and political system in which the means of production, distribution, and exchange are owned and controlled by the community as a whole, rather than by private individuals. Socialists advocate for the elimination of private property and the establishment of collective ownership, with the ultimate goal of creating a more egalitarian society.

On the other hand, corporatism (also known as corporativism) is an economic and political system that seeks to promote cooperation and collaboration between business, labor, and government. In a corporatist system, industries and professions are organized into interest groups, known as corporates, which have a direct input into policymaking processes. The role of the state is to mediate and balance the interests of these groups to ensure overall economic stability and growth.

A key distinction between socialism and corporatism is that socialism advocates for the abolition of private property, while corporatism acknowledges the importance of private property rights. In a corporatist system, the state plays a significant role in regulating and mediating relationships between businesses, workers, and consumers, but it does not seek to eliminate private enterprise altogether.

It's possible for a capitalist economy to exhibit some corporatist features, particularly in terms of regulation and industrial organization. For example, many countries with capitalist economies have established industry-specific regulatory bodies that work closely with corporate representatives to develop policies and address issues within their respective sectors. However, such systems would still fall short of fully realizing the corporatist ideal, as they do not entail the same degree of direct state control over industry and labor relations as found in true corporatist systems.

In summary, while there are similarities between corporatism and socialism, including a focus on collective action and regulation, the fundamental difference lies in the role of the state and private property. A capitalist economy can display some corporatist elements, but it remains fundamentally different from either socialism or corporatism in its core principles and goals.
response_b:
Corporatism and socialism are two distinct economic and political ideologies with significant differences. While both ideologies aim to address societal issues and improve the welfare of individuals, their approaches and outcomes differ in several ways.

Socialism is an economic system that advocates for collective ownership and control of resources, production, and distribution. Socialists believe that wealth and resources should be shared equally among all members of society, and they reject the idea of private property. Socialist systems typically involve central planning and government intervention in the economy to achieve social goals, such as income redistribution, social welfare programs, and public ownership of key industries.

On the other hand, corporatism is an economic and political system that emphasizes collaboration between business, labor, and government to promote economic growth and stability. Corporatism often involves tripartite negotiations between employers' associations, trade unions, and the government to resolve disputes and develop policies that benefit all parties. In contrast to socialism, corporatism does not necessarily advocate for collective ownership or control of resources, but rather seeks to balance the interests of businesses, workers, and the state through cooperation and negotiation.

It is possible for a capitalist economy to exhibit some corporatist features, particularly in countries with strong labor unions and employer organizations. In these cases, the government may play a more active role in facilitating negotiations and mediating disputes between businesses and unions. However, it is essential to note that corporatism does not inherently contradict capitalist principles; instead, it aims to reconcile the competing interests of various stakeholders within a capitalist framework.

In summary, while socialism and corporatism share some similarities, such as a focus on social welfare and equality, they differ fundamentally in their approach to resource allocation and economic organization. Capitalist economies can exhibit corporatist features, but this does not necessarily make them socialist. The extent to which a capitalist economy exhibits corporatist characteristics depends on the specific institutional and policy arrangements in place.

prompt: How can I write a compelling story about an investigation? Include key details and elements to include, and how to keep the reader engaged.
response_a:
Writing a compelling story about an investigation involves several key details and elements that you should consider. Here's a guide on what to include and how to keep your readers engaged:

1. Introduce your protagonist: Start by introducing your investigator, whether it's a seasoned detective or an amateur sleuth. Give them some backstory and personality traits that will help readers connect with them.

2. Set the scene: Create a vivid picture of the location where the crime took place. Use sensory language to bring the setting to life, such as describing the smells, sounds, and sights. This will help readers feel like they're there.

3. Establish the crime: Describe the nature of the crime in detail, including any clues or evidence left behind. Be sure to make it clear who the victim is and what happened to them.

4. Build tension: As the investigation progresses, introduce new suspects and red herrings to keep the reader guessing. Use pacing and suspense to build tension and keep readers engaged.

5. Develop the suspects: Flesh out each suspect with their own backstory and motivations. Show how they might have committed the crime or why they would want to.

6. Drop twists: Keep readers on their toes by throwing unexpected twists into the plot. These could be revelations about the victim, the investigator, or the suspects.

7. Resolve the case: End the story with a satisfying conclusion that ties up all loose ends. Make sure the culprit is revealed in a way that feels logical and believable.

To keep your readers engaged throughout the story, use descriptive language, dialogue, and action to break up long stretches of exposition. Alternate between scenes of investigation and moments of reflection or personal drama for the investigator. Finally, use cliffhangers at the end of chapters to leave readers wanting more.
response_b:
A compelling story about an investigation should have several key details and elements that will engage the reader from beginning to end. Here are some tips:

1. Introduce the crime: Start your story with a vivid description of the crime scene. Use sensory details to help the reader visualize the scene and feel the tension. Be sure to include any clues or evidence that may be important later in the investigation.

2. Introduce the detective: Give the reader a sense of who your detective is. What motivates them? What makes them unique? Are they experienced, or relatively new to the job?

3. Establish the stakes: Explain why this case is so important. Is there a high profile figure involved? Is there a history of similar crimes in the area? Is the victim someone particularly beloved by the community?

4. Develop the suspects: As the investigation progresses, introduce potential suspects. Each one should have their own backstory, motive, and alibi. The detective's interviews with each suspect should reveal new information, leading to further twists and turns in the case.

5. Build suspense: Keep the reader guessing by dropping hints and red herrings along the way. Don't give everything away at once - instead, slowly reveal clues and evidence as the investigation unfolds.

6. Create obstacles: Make the investigation difficult for the detective. Maybe there's a shortage of resources, or a high-ranking official is interfering with the case. Perhaps the detective themselves has a personal connection to the case that complicates matters.

7. Resolve the mystery: At the end of the story, make sure the resolution is satisfying but not too predictable. The detective should use all the clues and evidence gathered throughout the investigation to solve the crime. There should be a clear explanation for how the culprit was caught.

8. End on a strong note: Wrap up the story with a powerful closing line that leaves the reader feeling satisfied. This could be a reflection on the case, a poignant moment with the detective, or a final revelation that ties everything together.

By following these tips, you'll create a gripping and engaging story about an investigation that will keep readers on the edge of their seats until the very end.

However, they still sold Spanish stamps if required and between 1889 and 1898 the post office sold Gibraltar stamps valued in pesetas as this was the currency in circulation.

For the first fifty years, the Gibraltar Post Office had responsibility for the post office not only in Gibraltar but also for the British postal service in Morocco. This ended in 1907.

In 2005 the Gibraltar Post Office was granted the title of "Royal" by Her Majesty the Queen. Gibraltar is the only Commonwealth or British Overseas Territory post office outside the United Kingdom that bears this title. Gibraltar has traditional red pillar boxes and the tops are also frequently painted black.

The Post Office continues to provide some traditional services and was still using benefit books after they were abandoned in the United Kingdom, while there is also a special philatelic counter to sell the commemorative stamps.

The Post office provides a next day delivery service to the community with letters posted before 07.00 that day in any of the 30+ pillar boxes located in Gibraltar delivered same day. As the official designated postal operator by the UPU (Universal Postal Union) it has a universal service obligation to deliver mail to every Gibraltar resident and provide an international mail service to all UPU member countries worldwide (192 member countries)

Letter post

In September of that year, the Government stated that there were no plans to reopen either Post Office; Minister Joe Bossano explained there had been a proposal to house Savings Bank outlets in the premises but that when the money generated was considered, it was found not to be financially viable.

prompt: What is the history of the stole, and what role did it play in religious ceremonies throughout the ages?
response_a:
The stole is a liturgical garment worn by clergy members during religious ceremonies. Its origins can be traced back to the early Christian Church in the fourth century AD. At that time, deacons would wear a simple cloth called an orarion around their necks as a symbol of their office. This cloth was later adapted into a longer, more elaborate garment known as the stole.

In the Middle Ages, the stole became an important part of the liturgy, particularly in the Roman Catholic Church. It served both practical and symbolic purposes. On one hand, the stole helped distinguish the clergy from the laity by providing a visible sign of their ordained status. On the other hand, it also represented the authority and responsibility of the clergy to teach and preach the Gospel.

During religious ceremonies, the stole would be worn around the neck and draped over the left shoulder, with the ends hanging down the back. In some traditions, the stole might be worn in different colors depending on the occasion. For example, a white stole might be worn for baptisms or weddings, while a purple stole might be worn during Lent.

Over time, the design and materials used to make the stole have evolved. Originally made of plain linen or wool, today's stoles may be made of silk, velvet, or other luxurious fabrics, often decorated with intricate embroidery or embellishments.

In addition to its use in Christian liturgy, the stole has also been adopted by other religions. For example, in Orthodox Judaism, the stole-like garment known as the tallit katan is worn under regular clothing as a reminder of one's religious obligations. Similarly, in Tibetan Buddhism, the kasaya is a robe-like garment worn by monks and nuns that serves a similar function as the stole.

Overall, the stole has played an important role in religious ceremonies throughout the ages, serving as a symbol of authority, dignity, and devotion. Whether worn by Christian clergy, Jewish rabbis, or Buddhist monks, it continues to be a powerful reminder of the sacred nature of these traditions.
response_b:
The stole is a liturgical vestment that has been used in Christian religious ceremonies for over a thousand years. Its origins can be traced back to the Byzantine Empire, where it was known as an omophorion or phemelon. The omophorion was a long, rectangular cloth worn by Eastern Orthodox bishops and priests during worship services. It was draped over the shoulders like a yoke or crossbar (omos) and represented the burden of pastoral care that clergy carried for their flock.

I would guess even the most brilliant, experienced, educated-about-teens parent has felt the same sentiments as you about their teenager's behavior: "I don't know why or what to do." During the 18th and 19th centuries, aloe was one of the most frequently prescribed medications. Although oral consumption of aloe for constipation is no longer advised due to potential adverse effects, topical application of aloe gel, which comprises glycoproteins and polysaccharides that promote healing by reducing pain, inflammation, and accelerating skin regeneration, continues to gain popularity. Studies indicate that burn sites treated with aloe gel heal faster than those treated with traditional medications like silver sulfadiazine, with some reports indicating an average healing time reduction of nearly nine days. Nonetheless, the efficacy of aloe in promoting wound healing remains contentious, with some research suggesting that it may delay healing instead. Aloe gel is most beneficial for minor burns and skin irritations and should not be applied to open wounds.

prompt: What are some of the most important factors that influence investor decisions?
response_a:
1. Financial Performance: The most critical factor that influences investor decisions is the financial performance of the company. Investors analyze a company's income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements to determine its profitability, liquidity, and solvency. They look for trends in revenue growth, net income margins, return on equity (ROE), and debt-to-equity ratios.

2. Market Trends: Investors also consider broader market trends, such as economic indicators, interest rates, inflation, and geopolitical events. They assess how these factors may impact the industry and the specific company they are considering investing in.

3. Management Team: A strong management team with a proven track record is crucial in building confidence among investors. Investors evaluate the leadership skills, experience, and strategic vision of the CEO, CFO, and other key executives.

4. Industry Analysis: Investors study the competitive landscape of the industry, including the size and growth potential of the market, the regulatory environment, and the major players. They identify the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats facing the company and the industry as a whole.

5. Valuation: Before making an investment decision, investors conduct a thorough valuation analysis of the company. They use various methods, such as discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis, price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, and price-to-book (P/B) ratio, to determine the fair value of the stock.

6. Risk Assessment: Investors weigh the potential risks associated with the investment opportunity against the expected returns. They consider factors such as operational risks, legal and regulatory risks, credit risks, and market risks.

7. Competitive Advantage: Finally, investors evaluate the company's competitive advantage, including its unique products or services, brand reputation, intellectual property, and customer base. They assess whether the company has a sustainable competitive advantage that will enable it to maintain its market position over time.

Investment decisions involve complex and multifaceted evaluations, taking into account both qualitative and quantitative factors. By analyzing these factors, investors can make informed decisions that align with their investment objectives and risk tolerance.

prompt: What are some tips for running in the winter months? Consider factors such as clothing, diet, and overall training plan.
response_a:
Running in the winter months can be challenging due to colder temperatures, snow, ice, and shorter daylight hours. However, with proper preparation, it's possible to continue your running routine and even enjoy the winter season. Here are some tips for running during winter:

1. Dress appropriately: Layering is key when running in cold weather. Wear a base layer made of moisture-wicking fabric to keep you dry, followed by an insulating layer to trap heat, and a windproof and waterproof outer layer to protect against the elements. Don't forget to wear a hat, gloves, and warm socks.

2. Adjust your diet: Eating foods high in carbohydrates before running will provide your body with the energy it needs to stay warm. Also, make sure to drink enough water to prevent dehydration, as you may not feel as thirsty in the cold.

3. Plan your route carefully: Running on salted roads or paths can be slippery, so choose your route wisely. If there's snow or ice, consider using Yaktrax or similar devices to add traction to your shoes.

4. Modify your training plan: Shorten your runs or take them indoors if the conditions are too dangerous. Focus on speed workouts and hill repeats to improve your fitness without putting yourself at risk.

5. Stay motivated: Winter can be demotivating, but finding a running buddy, joining a virtual race, or listening to upbeat music can help keep you motivated and accountable.

6. Be aware of hypothermia: Hypothermia is a serious risk in extremely cold weather. To avoid it, dress appropriately, start your run warm, and bring extra layers just in case. Know the signs of hypothermia (shivering, confusion, slurred speech) and seek medical attention immediately if you experience any symptoms.

Remember, safety should always come first when running in winter. Always prioritize your health and wellbeing over pushing yourself too hard. With these tips, you can have a successful and enjoyable winter running season!
response_b:
Running in the winter can be challenging due to colder temperatures, snow, ice, and shorter daylight hours. Here are some tips to help you prepare and stay safe during this season:

Clothing:
- Dress in layers: Start with a moisture-wicking base layer, followed by an insulating middle layer, and a waterproof and breathable outer layer. This will help regulate your body temperature and keep you dry.
- Wear warm accessories: Don't forget to protect your extremities! Wear a hat, gloves or mittens, and a neck warmer to prevent frostbite and hypothermia.
- Reflective gear: If running in low light conditions, wear reflective clothing or add reflective strips to your outfit to increase visibility.

Diet:
- Stay hydrated: Even though it may not feel as hot outside, dehydration is still a concern in cold weather. Drink enough water before, during, and after your runs to replace fluids lost through sweating and breathing.
- Eat carbs: Carbohydrates provide quick energy for your workouts, especially in cold weather when your body burns more calories to stay warm. Consume complex carbohydrates like whole grains, fruits, and vegetables.
- Protein: Protein helps repair and build muscles, which is essential for preventing injury and recovery. Incorporate lean proteins like chicken, fish, and legumes into your diet.

Overall Training Plan:
- Adjust your pace: Running on slippery surfaces like ice and snow requires more caution and effort. Slow down your pace to maintain proper form and avoid falls.
- Shorten your runs: Shorter days and colder temperatures make it harder to motivate yourself to run long distances. Focus on quality over quantity and incorporate speed work and hill repeats into your routine.
- Cross-training: Add strength training exercises, yoga, and indoor cycling classes to your weekly routine to improve flexibility, balance, and core stability. These activities will also help prevent injury and promote overall fitness.

Remember, safety should always come first. Check weather forecasts and trail conditions before heading out, carry a cellphone, and let someone know your route and expected return time. Happy winter running!

prompt: What is the difference between a station wagon and a SUV?
response_a:
While both station wagons and SUVs can serve as practical vehicles for transporting people and cargo, there are some key differences:

1. Body style: A station wagon, also known as an estate car or a shoot-brake, is typically based on a sedan body design with a large rear trunk area that can be accessed through a tailgate or side doors. In contrast, an SUV (Sports Utility Vehicle) has a more boxy and upright body shape, often with four-wheel drive capabilities and higher ground clearance for off-road driving.

2. Passenger capacity: Station wagons generally have seating for up to five passengers in two or three rows, while many SUVs offer more spacious interiors with seating for seven or more passengers across multiple rows.

3. Cargo space: Station wagons prioritize cargo space over passenger volume, often featuring fold-down rear seats and a flat load floor for easy loading and unloading of bulky items. SUVs may also offer ample cargo space, but they often prioritize passenger comfort and convenience over maximum cargo capacity.

4. Driving dynamics: Station wagons typically offer better handling and a smoother ride than most SUVs due to their lower center of gravity and lighter overall weight. However, some high-performance SUVs can offer similar driving experiences.

5. Fuel efficiency: Station wagons tend to be more fuel-efficient than comparable-sized SUVs because of their lighter weight and sleeker aerodynamic designs. This can result in lower operating costs over time.

Ultimately, the choice between a station wagon and an SUV will depend on individual preferences and needs regarding passenger capacity, cargo space, driving experience, and lifestyle requirements.
response_b:
While both station wagons and SUVs serve as transportation vehicles, there are some key differences between the two:

1. Body Style: A station wagon, also known as an estate car or a shoot-brake, has a traditional sedan body with a extended rear section that provides more cargo space. It usually has four doors and a roofline that slopes downwards towards the back. On the other hand, an SUV (Sports Utility Vehicle) has a boxy, truck-like design with a raised ride height, typically featuring four or five doors.

2. Purpose: Station wagons were originally designed to carry people and their luggage on long journeys. They provide ample space for passengers in the front and back seats, as well as for cargo in the extended boot. In contrast, SUVs were initially created for off-road driving, but they have evolved into more versatile vehicles that offer a higher seating position, better ground clearance, and all-wheel drive capabilities for handling rough terrain.

3. Performance: Due to their different purposes, station wagons and SUVs also vary in terms of performance. Generally speaking, station wagons prioritize comfort, handling, and fuel efficiency over raw power. They often come equipped with smaller engines and lower suspension systems, making them ideal for cruising on highways and city streets. In contrast, SUVs tend to have larger engines and more powerful drivetrains to tackle challenging terrains, although this can result in less efficient fuel consumption.

4. Price: The cost of owning either vehicle also depends on its intended use. Station wagons are generally less expensive than comparable-sized SUVs due to their simpler designs and lower manufacturing costs. However, some premium station wagons may be priced similarly to luxury SUVs because of their advanced features and high-end materials.

In summary, while both station wagons and SUVs provide practical solutions for transporting people and cargo, they differ significantly in terms of style, purpose, performance, and price point. Ultimately, the choice between the two comes down to personal preferences, needs, and budget constraints.

Concerns about beef liver
Many people may avoid eating beef liver due to health concerns, including cholesterol, toxicity, and an overload of iron.

Some key characteristics of clusters include:

1. Concentration: Clusters are densely populated with related organizations operating within a relatively small geographic area.

2. Interdependence: Members of a cluster rely on each other for inputs, services, and resources.

3. Learning: Clusters foster learning and innovation through the exchange of knowledge and best practices among member firms.

4. Networks: Clusters are characterized by strong social networks among members, facilitating communication and collaboration.

5. Competition: Despite the interdependence, competition also exists within clusters, driving innovation and efficiency.

An example of a cluster is Silicon Valley, which is home to many technology companies such as Apple, Google, and Facebook. These firms collaborate and compete with each other, contributing to the growth and success of the region's economy. Another example is the biotech industry in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where leading firms such as Biogen and Genzyme are located.

In contrast, a group is a collection of individuals who come together based on shared interests, values, or goals. Groups can be formal or informal and may operate across geographic boundaries. Unlike clusters, groups do not necessarily involve businesses or institutions, but rather focus on individual interaction and communication. Key characteristics of groups include:

1. Shared identity: Group members share a common sense of identity, such as a shared background, culture, or profession.

response_b:

These interconnected businesses can benefit from economies of scale, knowledge spillovers, and increased competitiveness. For example, Silicon Valley in California is a well-known technology cluster that includes companies like Apple, Google, and Intel. Other examples include Boston's biotech cluster, Wall Street's financial services cluster, and Detroit's automotive cluster.

In contrast, a group is a collection of individuals or organizations with shared interests, goals, or purposes. Groups may be formal or informal, temporary or permanent, and can exist within or outside of organizations. Members of a group typically interact and collaborate to achieve common objectives. For instance, a project team in a company is a group working towards completing a specific task or delivering a product. Professional associations, social clubs, and interest groups are other examples of groups.

The key difference between clusters and groups is that clusters primarily focus on economic benefits and industry synergies, while groups prioritize collaboration and shared goals among members. Clusters emerge naturally due to proximity and shared resources, whereas groups are formed intentionally by individuals who share common interests or needs. However, there is some overlap between these concepts as clusters may also lead to the formation of groups, such as trade associations or networking events for businesses in a particular cluster.

Similarities between clusters and groups include the potential for network effects, which refer to the idea that the value of a product or service increases as more users adopt it. For groups, organizations can facilitate collaboration, communication, and knowledge exchange among members to improve performance, increase productivity, and enhance decision-making. On the other hand, clusters and groups can also face competition, rivalry, and resource constraints, which require strategic management and coordination

The coronavirus and resulting increase in government regulation will continue to cause detrimental economic impact to businesses and individuals. This adverse impact on revenues and expenses will create challenges in meeting obligations under contracts. A properly drafted force majeure clause can help, but what happens if the force majeure clause is too narrow or the contract simply does not include one? Companies should know they may still have a legal basis under Oklahoma law to avoid or limit contractual obligations that have become impossible or impracticable to perform.

Impossibility and impracticability are closely related, but technically distinguishable, doctrines. Impossibility is a common law defense while impracticability is a Uniform Commercial Code defense. Oklahoma courts generally do not distinguish between impossibility and impracticability because the terms are of equal legal effect. In either case, a party's performance is excused if it has become "impossible" or "totally unreasonable or impracticable" due to an event outside of the party's control and that the party could not reasonably foresee when executing the contract.

A duty is impossible to perform if it cannot be accomplished by any means. Impracticability requires extreme and unreasonable difficulty, expense, injury, or loss. As a result, changes in market forces do not render performance impracticable unless far outside the normal range, because they are the sort of risk that commercial contracts are intended to cover. Whereas severe shortages due to exigencies such as war, embargo, local crop failure, or unforeseen shutdown of major sources of supply that cause a marked increase in cost or prevent performance may render performance impracticable. Even when performance is impossible or impracticable, parties must use reasonable efforts to surmount any obstacles to performance and must continue to perform those portions of obligations that are possible or practicable.

For example, courts in Oklahoma have held that it was impossible or impracticable: for an employer to comply with the terms of a settlement agreement requiring it to use the plaintiff as a back-up machine operator, where the company stopped using the machine and there was no need for an operator or backup operator; for a lessor to restore a tornado-demolished hotel, where the hotel could not be reasonably reconstructed or the defendant could not obtain the necessary materials due to a state of war; and for a railroad to continue shipping grain, where the railroad ceased operations following the construction of a dam that flooded 19 miles of tracks and which would have cost $25 million in today's dollars to relocate.

In contrast, an Oklahoma court has held that it was not impossible or impracticable for a defendant to purchase natural gas at the "take-or-pay" contract price despite an extreme deviation between that price and the market value of the gas caused by governmental regulation and financial hardship, because "a more than twofold increase in the cost of performing [did] not alter the essential nature of performance."

The event that makes performance impossible or impracticable cannot be reasonably foreseeable when the parties made the contract. An event is deemed foreseeable if the parties allocated the risk of its occurrence in the contract.

Oklahoma courts have applied these principles to hold: the parties to a settlement agreement requiring the defendant to use the plaintiff as a back-up machine operator reasonably assumed there would be a continued need for operators and back-up operators; a basic assumption of the parties' shipping agreement was that if the railroad ceased to exist, the contract would be dissolved and the railroad's nonperformance would be excused; and the parties to a lease never contemplated their agreement to repair included rebuilding a leased hotel after a tornado destroyed it.

On the other hand, courts in Oklahoma have held: the parties to a swine purchasing agreement reasonably foresaw the market price could fall to one-third or one-sixth of the agreed floor price; a consultant and casino developer "had every reason to anticipate" that the developer's subsidiary could fail to obtain required financing, where the contract acknowledged the risk that pre-development opportunities may not lead to permanent opportunities; a gas-purchaser assumed the risk of an extreme disparity between the contract price and the market value of gas when it agreed to purchase gas at a fixed price subject to redetermination based on the highest price paid in a four-county area; and "world-wide glut of oil, a severe national economic recession, foreign commodity competition, abnormally warm weather during 19821983, price-induced consumer energy conservation and a sudden, wholly unexpected, unanticipated and unforeseeable change in the natural gas market because of the worldwide glut of oil were exactly the type of risks that business contracts made at fixed prices are intended to cover.ii

The coronavirus and related government action are clearly outside of companies' control and not something they could have reasonably foreseen. The absence of a force majeure clause may actually strengthen the argument that the risk of a pandemic was not allocated in a contract. As a result, we expect companies' ability to successfully assert these defenses will primarily turn on the extent to which performing would actually cause extreme and unreasonable difficulty, expense, injury, or loss. This is a fact-intensive inquiry and must be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Companies must use reasonable efforts to overcome any obstacles to performance and must continue to perform those portions of their obligations that are not impossible or impracticable.

Companies should also be aware of the related common law defense of frustration of purpose. Even if performance likely remains possible or practicable, companies may avoid or limit their contractual obligations if coronavirus or related government action has substantially frustrated the principal purpose of the contract. It is not enough for the contract to become less profitable or for the affected party to sustain a loss; the frustration must be so severe that it cannot fairly be regarded as within the risks assumed under the contract. For example, one court held the principal purpose of a car rental franchise agreement was not impaired by a hurricane because rental cars remained intact and the franchise conducted some business immediately following the hurricane.

Even in the absence of a force majeure clause or strong common law defense, companies can still take steps to protect themselves, such as reviewing their contract's termination clause or negotiating with the other party to amend or suspend performance.

As the coronavirus and governmental response continue to unfold, companies and their counter-parties should expect to face increased challenges to performing their contractual obligations. Companies should be proactive and begin the process now of carefully reviewing their contracts to determine their rights and obligations as to force majeure (and termination). Even in the absence of a force majeure clause, companies should be aware they may have a legal basis under Oklahoma law to avoid or limit contractual obligations that have become impossible or impracticable to perform. Companies that intend to rely on these defenses must take all reasonable steps to meet their contractual obligations and continue to perform those portions of their obligations that are not impossible or impracticable.

prompt: What is the optimal time to take a multivitamin according to recent medical research?
response_a:
According to recent medical research, the optimal time to take a multivitamin may vary depending on the specific nutrients in the supplement. Here's what we know:

1. Vitamin D: Recent studies suggest that taking vitamin D with a meal can improve its absorption. Since many multivitamins contain vitamin D, it's best to take your supplement with breakfast or lunch.

2. B-vitamins: B-vitamins, including folic acid and B12, are often taken together as part of a multivitamin. These vitamins are water-soluble and can be easily flushed out of the body if not absorbed properly. Taking them with food, especially a source of protein, can help prevent this.

3. Iron: If you're taking an iron supplement, it's best to avoid taking it with calcium-rich foods (such as milk or cheese) or antacids, as these can interfere with iron absorption. Instead, take your iron supplement with a glass of orange juice or another source of vitamin C, which can help increase iron absorption.

4. Magnesium: Some people have reported diarrhea when taking magnesium supplements, which can be alleviated by spreading out your doses throughout the day. You might consider splitting your multivitamin into two doses instead of taking it all at once.

In general, it's best to take your multivitamin with a meal to ensure proper absorption and reduce any potential stomach discomfort. However, if you experience any negative side effects from your current regimen, such as nausea or diarrhea, talk to your doctor or a registered dietitian about alternative options. They can help you find a multivitamin that meets your needs and works well for your body.
response_b:

However, a study published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2020 found that taking certain vitamins and minerals with meals can improve their absorption. Specifically, vitamins A, D, E, and K, as well as calcium and iron, are best absorbed when taken with a meal that contains fat.

On the other hand, water-soluble vitamins such as B complex vitamins and vitamin C are not stored in the body and need to be consumed regularly. These vitamins can be taken at any time of day, but it's recommended to spread them out throughout the day for consistent levels in the bloodstream.

Overall, it's best to consult with a healthcare provider or registered dietitian to determine the specific needs and timing of vitamin supplementation based on individual health conditions and goals.

Albert Delin  (17 April 1712, Ath – 26 Nov 1771, Tournai; also known as Albertus Delin) was a harpsichord maker in the Low Countries.

Biography
Born in Ath in Southern Netherlands (now in Belgium), he soon moved to the nearby town of Tournai to practice his trade. Little is known of his training but a remarkable number of his instruments have survived. His building style is quite contrary to his more famous contemporaries, like his neighbours Dulckens in Antwerp, the Hass family in Hamburg or the Taskins of Paris, that at the time created complex machines with an extensive variety of registers and knee levers. Delin's surviving instruments are simple, reminiscent of the old Ruckers instruments of a century before and of good workmanship as witnessed by the number of surviving instruments.

Surviving instruments
Two surviving harpsichords (1750 and1768), both have a single manual and have only two 8' choirs and a buff stop, with all battens protruding through the instruments side, similar to original Ruckers instruments.
Kottick mentions four bentside spinets (1763, 1765, 1766, 1770), all with a single 8' choir.  A colorful fifth bentside spinet signed "A.D. 1738" and bearing a rose with the initials AD, has been attributed to him as well.
Three clavicytheria (1751, 1752, 1760), strung like his harpsichords with two 8' registers, and guidebattens protruding through the cheek. The clavicytheria have an elegant pivot mechanism of Delins' own design, needing no spring action and only gravity for the return. Chung describes Delins clavicytherium thus: "[he] succeeded in overcoming the difficulties of building an upright harpsichord better than any other builder. His three instruments, which are considered by many to be the finest of all surviving clavicytheria, have an amazingly fine touch that is achieved by a special action that upon the release of the keys allows the jacks to return without the need of springs or additional weights."
The last surviving instrument is even more old fashioned than the rest, a small, hexagonal, octave spinet (1750).

Decor of the instruments
Delin's original case decor seems to have been simple, but some of his instruments later received "makeovers". Most notably his 1760 clavicytherium, was retrofitted with an extravagant gilded, rococo door. The 1738 spinet is elaborately painted with a forest scene on the inside of the lid, while the case is covered with a menagerie of monkeys playing musical instruments.

The soundboard paintings in Delin's instruments are typical Flemish floral motifs, with visible outlines, flat coloring and little detail, a style similar to the Ruckers.

prompt: What are some interesting facts about twins?
response_a:
1. Identical twins (monozygotic) share the same DNA, while fraternal twins (dizygotic) have separate DNA since they develop from two fertilized eggs.

2. The rate of identical twinning is around 3-4 times higher in some populations, such as Nigerians and Africans of Cameroonian descent, compared to Caucasians.

3. Twins can be conjoined (Siamese), meaning they share bodily structures or organs.

4. Some sets of twins experience a condition called "vanishing twin syndrome," where one embryo stops developing early on in pregnancy and is eventually absorbed by the other.

5. Twins have been reported to have different personalities, despite sharing genetic material. This may be due to environmental factors during development or after birth.

6. In rare cases, twins can have different fathers, a phenomenon known as heteropaterny or superfecundation, which occurs when a woman conceives twins from two different partners around the same time.

7. Twin studies have helped researchers understand how genes contribute to various traits and diseases, as twins provide a unique opportunity to compare nature versus nurture influences.

8. Famous historical twins include the Wright brothers, Wilbur and Orville, who invented the airplane together, and the Karamazov Brothers, four fictional characters created by Russian author Fyodor Dostoyevsky.

9. The world's oldest living twins, Olga and Lidya Mukhiny, were born in Russia in 1923 and celebrated their 106th birthday in March 2021.

10. A set of quadruplets, known as the Dionne quintuplets, were born in Canada in 1934 and became famous for being the first set of quintuplets to survive infancy. Their story sparked controversy over whether it was ethical to display them as a tourist attraction.
response_b:
1. Identical twins (monozygotic) develop from a single fertilized egg splitting into two embryos, while fraternal twins (dizygotic) develop from two separate eggs being fertilized by two sperm cells.

2. Twins can have different birth weights, even if they are identical. This is due to factors such as the position in the womb and access to nutrients.

3. Studies have shown that identical twins raised apart still tend to have similar personality traits, suggesting that genetics play a significant role in shaping personality.

8. Twin studies have contributed significantly to our understanding of genetics, allowing researchers to identify specific genes associated with various diseases and traits.

9. The world's oldest living twins, Zoze Neno Cristovam dos Santos and Jesuino Moura Dos Santos, are Brazilian brothers born on June 23, 1917. They celebrated their 102nd birthday in 2019.

It’s worth a visit year-round for the many garlic-infused products for sale (ice cream, jelly, popcorn) and the subtle but pervasive scent of garlic that led Will Rogers to say, “Gilroy is the only town I know where you can marinate a steak by hanging it on the clothesline.” When pairing with garlic-heavy dishes, take into account which of its flavors are taking center stage.

Pungent
When cut, raw garlic releases sulfurous compounds that create its characteristically complex pungency. A high-acid white wine can cut the bite of garlic in much the same way that citrus does in a salad dressing. Dry Furmint (the primary grape in sweet Tokaji Aszú wines) brims with sharp citrus, boasts a saline streak and hints at garlic’s best pal, ginger. Grab it when you can find it.

Tip: When mincing or crushing garlic, wait at least 10 seconds before adding to anything acidic or to a hot pan. Acid and heat inhibit the enzymatic process from which raw garlic gets its power.
Spicy
Garlic doesn’t contain capsaicin, the source of tongue-searing heat in chili peppers, but if you chew a clove of raw garlic, your mouth will hardly know the difference. However, while capsaicin is difficult to pair with red wine, garlic welcomes wines with complementary spicy flavors. With its charcuterie and pepper notes, cool-climate Syrah—northern Rhône, Adelaide Hills, Central Coast California—is a natural choice.

Sweet

Oloroso Sherry is usually a dry wine, but its rich texture and intensely nutty, oxidized flavors give it a mouth-filling roundness that plays well with dishes that straddle sweet and savory.

Umami
This fifth flavor is deeply savory (think dry-aged meat, blue cheese, mushrooms), and roasted and black garlic, in particular, are full of it. Garlic’s umami quality is why it adds such depth to so many dishes around the world. Tannins can clash with umami, so try a crisp and low-tannin red like those from Austria’s Zweigelt grape. It makes easy-drinking wines full of red fruit and a whiff of garlic-friendly black pepper.

prompt: What is the difference between stupidity and ignorance?
response_a:
Stupidity refers to a lack of intelligence or common sense, which can lead to making poor decisions, not learning from mistakes, and having difficulty understanding concepts. Stupidity is often seen as a permanent trait that cannot be easily changed.

Ignorance, on the other hand, refers to a lack of knowledge or information about a particular subject or topic. Ignorance can be remedied through education, learning, and acquiring new information. Unlike stupidity, ignorance does not necessarily indicate a lack of intelligence but rather a lack of exposure to certain ideas or experiences.

In summary, while both stupidity and ignorance involve a lack of something (intelligence or knowledge), stupidity suggests an inherent flaw in one's cognitive abilities, whereas ignorance implies a lack of information or experience.
response_b: Ignorance refers to the lack of knowledge or information about a particular subject or topic. Stupidity, on the other hand, goes beyond ignorance and refers to a lack of intelligence or common sense in using the knowledge that is already available. In other words, while ignorance can be remedied through education and learning, stupidity is more deeply ingrained and resistant to change. Ignorant people can become informed with the right guidance, but stupid people may continue making poor decisions despite having access to accurate information.

2. Robusta Coffee: Robusta coffee makes up around 30-40% of global coffee production and is known for its strong and bold flavor. It has a high caffeine content and a slightly bitter taste. Robusta coffee beans are smaller and rounder than Arabica beans and have a less dense texture.

3. Liberica Coffee: Liberica coffee is a rare variety that comes from the Philippines, Indonesia, and Africa. It has a smoky, bacony flavor with hints of spice and chocolate. The beans are long and twisted in shape, giving them an unusual appearance.

4. Excelsa Coffee: Excelsa coffee is a lesser-known variety that is grown in Southeast Asia and South America. It has a light and nutty flavor with a hint of sweetness. The beans are similar in size to Robusta but have a more complex aroma.

5. Maragogype Coffee: Maragogype coffee produces the largest coffee beans in the world, sometimes reaching up to twice the size of Arabica beans. The flavor is mild and nutty with a low acidity level. It is mainly grown in Brazil and Central America.

Overall, the choice of coffee depends on personal preference as each type has its unique flavor profile. Arabica coffee is generally preferred for its delicate flavor, while Robusta coffee is favored for its stronger taste. Rarer varieties like Liberica and Maragogype coffee offer unique flavor experiences for those looking to explore beyond the usual options.

prompt: What are some ways to make money in business?
response_a:
1. Sell products or services: This is the most straightforward way to generate income in business. Identify a need in the market and create a product or service that meets that need. Then, sell it to customers for a profit.

2. Charge fees for services: If you offer professional services such as consulting, coaching, or accounting, you can charge clients an hourly rate or a flat fee for your expertise.

3. Licensing and franchising: You can license your brand, products, or technology to other businesses for a royalty fee. Alternatively, you can franchise your business, allowing others to operate under your name for a fee.

4. Investments and dividends: If you own shares in a company, you can earn dividends when the company distributes profits to shareholders. Additionally, you may be able to sell your shares for a profit if the stock price increases.

5. Renting out property: If you own commercial or residential real estate, you can rent it out to tenants for a monthly rental fee.

6. Advertising and sponsorships: Businesses can earn money by selling advertising space on their websites, social media pages, or physical locations. They can also seek out sponsorship opportunities from brands looking to promote their products or services.

7. Mergers and acquisitions: In some cases, businesses can grow through merging with or acquiring another company. This strategy can lead to significant revenue gains if the acquired business is profitable.

8. Crowdfunding: Some entrepreneurs choose to fund their business ideas through crowdfunding platforms like Kickstarter or Indiegogo. These campaigns allow individuals to donate small amounts of money to support the project, often in exchange for rewards or equity in the company.

9. Government contracts: Certain types of businesses, particularly those providing goods or services to the government, can secure lucrative contracts through bidding processes.

10. Subscription-based models: More and more companies are adopting subscription-based pricing models, charging customers a recurring fee for access to ongoing services or products. This can provide a steady stream of revenue over time.
response_b:
1. Sell a product or service: This is the most traditional and straightforward way to generate revenue in any business. Identify a need or want in the market, create a solution, and sell it for a profit.

2. Licensing and franchising: Licensing involves granting another company the right to use your intellectual property (such as a trademark or patent) for a fee. Franchising allows another business to operate under your brand name and follow your established systems and processes for a fee.

3. Renting or leasing: If you own a physical asset such as real estate, equipment, or vehicles, consider renting or leasing them out to generate income.

4. Advertising and sponsorships: Businesses can earn money by selling advertising space on their website, social media channels, or physical locations. They can also charge for sponsoring events or products.

5. Investments: Businesses can invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, or other financial instruments to earn passive income.

6. Consulting and coaching: Use your expertise and knowledge to provide consulting services to other businesses or individuals for a fee.

7. Mergers and acquisitions: A company can grow through merging with or acquiring another business, which can result in increased revenue and assets.

8. Crowdfunding: Platforms like Kickstarter, Indiegogo, and GoFundMe allow entrepreneurs to raise capital from a large number of people in exchange for rewards or equity.

However, some brewers use small amounts of corn (known as adjuncts) for specific purposes, such as adding body and head retention. The most common type of corn used in beer is yellow corn, which is also commonly used in animal feed and ethanol production. Other types of corn, such as white, blue, and red corn, are less commonly used in beer but may be used by some artisanal brewers for their unique flavor profiles. Here are some examples:

1. Yellow Corn: This is the most commonly used type of corn in beer due to its high starch content, which helps to create body and mouthfeel. It is typically used in conjunction with other grains like barley or wheat.

2. White Corn: Also known as flint corn, this type of corn has a higher protein content than yellow corn and can contribute to a fuller-bodied beer. It is less commonly used due to its lower starch content.

3. Blue Corn: This type of corn is often used in traditional Native American beers and has a nutty, earthy flavor. It is also gluten-free due to a unique processing method called nixtamalization.

4. Red Corn: Also known as blood corn, this type of corn has a reddish-purple color and is often used in Mexican cuisine. In beer, it can add a slightly sweet and fruity flavor.

5. Heirloom Corn: Some brewers use heirloom varieties of corn, which can have unique flavor profiles based on their genetics. These beers are often more expensive and limited in availability due to the rarity of the corn.

Overall, while corn is not typically used as a primary ingredient in beer, it can be a useful adjunct for certain styles or purposes. Its use should be done sparingly and in balance with other flavors in the beer.

prompt: What is the difference between a class and an instance in OOP?
response_a:
A class in object-oriented programming (OOP) is a blueprint or a template that defines the properties and methods of an object. It serves as a prototype for creating objects with similar characteristics. In simple terms, a class is like a recipe that describes how to make a dish, while an object is like the actual dish made using the recipe.

An instance, on the other hand, is an object that is created based on a specific class. Instances have their own unique values for the properties defined in the class. They can also interact with each other through messages sent using the methods defined in the class. In short, an instance is like a particular dish prepared using the recipe provided by its corresponding class.

In summary, a class is a general concept or a type, while an instance is a specific occurrence or an object of that class.
response_b:
In Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), a class can be thought of as a blueprint or a template for creating objects, while an instance is a specific object created based on that class.

A class defines the properties (attributes) and behaviors (methods) that all objects of that type will have. For example, a Car class might have properties like make, model, and color, as well as methods for starting, stopping, and accelerating.

An instance, on the other hand, is a specific object with its own unique values for those properties. For instance, one Car instance might have a make of "Toyota", a model of "Corolla", and a color of "red". Each instance of a class has its own state, which is represented by its property values.

So, to summarize:

- A class is a general description of what an object can be and do.
- An instance is a specific object that conforms to the definition provided by the class.

He gasped and smiled when he saw me. "Oh, honey, you look like a princess! Go on, give us a twirl." He wound his finger in demonstration.

Rolling my eyes but smiling anyway, I obliged him, and admittedly did feel very princess-like as the blue fabric of my knee-length dress spun around me. Joel cheered me on, making me blush.

"Okay, okay, show's over," I said, looking at my watch. "We only have about ten minutes left."

"Dios mío, I didn't even realize," Joel said, as he rushed with the sweeper to the front of the gallery. "Did I forget anything?"

I took a quick tour around and didn't see anything amiss. Joel finished up sweeping the floor with only minutes to spare, and gave me a quick peck on the cheek before heading into the back room to get changed for the evening. While I waited for both him and my guest, I paced the gallery once again, eyeballing my paintings, whispering his name under my breath.

"Sheikh Rafiq Al-Zayn, Sheikh Rafiq Al-Zayn...." I turned with a whimper to Joel as he breezed past me to put the sweeper away. "These private exhibitions always make me so damn nervous, Joel. At least in a crowd, the pressure isn't entirely on me."

Joel stopped and turned back, dropping the sweeper on the floor. He opened up his big arms to me and held me in a tight, warm hug. Instantly my nerves started to calm.

"You've done this a hundred times, mami, and for all sorts of rich and powerful people. They love you! Look at you. You are a charming flower they want to put in a vase and take home. Tonight will be no different."

"You're the charmer," I said. "Thank you. I don't know how I would do this without you."

"Try the hummus before he gets here and eats all of it—it's incredible." Joel winked at me and picked up the sweeper, disappearing into the back room.

TWO

Two hours later and the hummus was gone. Despite my protests to keep everything as beautiful and perfect as it was when we set it all up, Joel couldn't help himself, not after the first hour of aimless waiting. After all, he'd come straight from work without stopping for dinner, and I didn't protest as he greedily scooped up the dip with leftover spiced pita chips straight from the bag.

We had set up some of the plain black chairs on either side of the snack table once our feet started to hurt. I looked across at him as he finished it up, chin in my hands. Joel gave me a satisfied wink as he licked his lips.

"I can't believe this," I mumbled. My heart felt like it weighed a thousand pounds. "Why can't rich people value anyone's time but their own?"

"A question for the ages," said Joel. "I wish I could say I was as surprised as you, but I've worked in too many high class restaurants to have any fantasies left about them.

Description
Gryllus firmus is very similar in appearance to other crickets found in the southeastern United States, the southeastern field cricket (Gryllus rubens) and the Texas field cricket (Gryllus texensis). It has a black head and prothorax, and a brown abdomen. It can be distinguished from these two species by the coloration and venation of the forewing, but more particularly, by its call. Males of this species chirp while males of the other two species trill.

Distribution and habitat
Gryllus firmus occurs in the coastal plain of the southeastern United States. Its range extends from Connecticut and New Hampshire to Florida and Texas. The long winged morph is migratory. It is replaced to the north and west of its range by the fall field cricket (Gryllus pennsylvanicus), and the two species hybridise to a limited extent where their ranges overlap. Its typical habitat is grassland, pasture, roadside verges and lawns on light, free-draining sandy soils.

Biology
Gryllus firmus exhibits wing polymorphism; some individuals have fully functional, long hind wings and others have short wings and cannot fly. Females of the latter morph have smaller flight muscles, greater ovarian development and produce more eggs, so the polymorphism adapts the cricket for either dispersal or reproduction. G. firmus is unusual among field crickets in laying a mixture of two types of egg. Some eggs develop immediately and take two to four weeks to hatch, while others have a diapause, with delayed hatching taking place after from five to twenty-eight weeks. Researchers have discovered the most distant active supermassive black hole to date with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The galaxy, CEERS 1019, existed about 570 million years after the big bang, and its black hole is less massive than any other yet identified in the early universe.

In addition to the black hole in CEERS 1019, the researchers identified two more black holes that are on the smaller side and existed 1 billion and 1.1 billion years after the big bang. JWST also identified eleven galaxies that existed when the universe was 470 million to 675 million years old. The evidence was provided by JWST's Cosmic Evolution Early Release Science (CEERS) Survey, led by Steven Finkelstein, a professor of astronomy at The University of Texas at Austin. The program combines JWST's highly detailed near- and mid-infrared images and data known as spectra, all of which were used to make these discoveries.

"Looking at this distant object with this telescope is a lot like looking at data from black holes that exist in galaxies near our own," said Rebecca Larson, a recent Ph.D. graduate at UT Austin, who led the study. "There are so many spectral lines to analyze!"

The team has published these results in several initial papers in a special edition of The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

CEERS 1019 is notable not only for how long ago it existed, but also how relatively little its black hole weighs. It clocks in around 9 million solar masses, far less than other black holes that also existed in the early universe and were detected by other telescopes. Those behemoths typically contain more than 1 billion times the mass of the sun -- and they are easier to detect because they are much brighter. The black hole within CEERS 1019 is more like the black hole at the center of our Milky Way galaxy, which is 4.6 million times the mass of the sun.

Though smaller, this black hole existed so much earlier that it is still difficult to explain how it formed so soon after the universe began. Researchers have long known that smaller black holes must have existed earlier in the universe, but it wasn't until JWST began observing that they were able to make definitive detections.

Not only could the team untangle which emissions in the spectrum are from the black hole and which are from its host galaxy, they could also pinpoint how much gas the black hole is ingesting and determine its galaxy's star-formation rate.

The team found this galaxy is ingesting as much gas as it can while also churning out new stars. They turned to the images to explore why that might be. Visually, CEERS 1019 appears as three bright clumps, not a single circular disk.

"We're not used to seeing so much structure in images at these distances," said CEERS team member Jeyhan Kartaltepe, an associate professor of astronomy at the Rochester Institute of Technology in New York. "A galaxy merger could be partly responsible for fueling the activity in this galaxy's black hole, and that could also lead to increased star formation."

These are only the first groundbreaking findings from the CEERS Survey.

"Until now, research about objects in the early universe was largely theoretical," Finkelstein said. "With Webb, not only can we see black holes and galaxies at extreme distances, we can now start to accurately measure them. That's the tremendous power of this telescope."

In the future, it's possible JWST's data may also be used to explain how early black holes formed, revising researchers' models of how black holes grew and evolved in the first several hundred million years of the universe's history.

The James Webb Space Telescope is an international program led by NASA with its partners, the European Space Agency and the Canadian Space Agency.

More Extremely Distant Black Holes and Galaxies

The CEERS Survey is expansive, and there is much more to explore. Team member Dale Kocevski of Colby College in Waterville, Maine, and the team quickly spotted another pair of small black holes in the data. The first, within galaxy CEERS 2782, was easiest to pick out. There isn't any dust obscuring JWST's view of it, so researchers could immediately determine when its black hole existed in the history of the universe -- only 1.1 billion years after the big bang. The second black hole, in galaxy CEERS 746, existed slightly earlier, 1 billion years after the big bang. Its bright accretion disk, a ring made up of gas and dust that encircles its supermassive black hole, is still partially clouded by dust.

"The central black hole is visible, but the presence of dust suggests it might lie within a galaxy that is also furiously pumping out stars," Kocevski explained.

Like the one in CEERS 1019, the two other newly described black holes (in galaxies CEERS 2782 and CEERS 746) are also "light weights" -- at least when compared with previously known supermassive black holes at these distances. They are only about 10 million times the mass of the sun.

"Researchers have long known that there must be lower mass black holes in the early universe. Webb is the first observatory that can capture them so clearly," Kocevski said. "Now we think that lower mass black holes might be all over the place, waiting to be discovered."

"Webb was the first to detect some of these galaxies," explained Fujimoto. "This set, along with other distant galaxies we may identify in the future, might change our understanding of star formation and galaxy evolution throughout cosmic history," he added.

In vitro cells have helped us to attain a deeper understanding of functions and mechanisms conserved in the course of evolution. Toxicology studies are inevitable in drug discovery, pesticide development, and many other fields that directly interact with human beings. The proper involvement and regulatory steps that have been taken by animal ethical societies in different parts of the world resulted in the reduced in vivo use of mammals in toxicological studies. Nowadays, invertebrate cell lines also play an important role in toxicology testing. This review analyzes the cause and consequence of insect in vitro models in toxicology studies.
Across centuries, research involving animals has contributed significantly to the progress of biomedical sciences. However, the use of animals in research experiments became a subject of controversy. The pain and suffering experienced by animals had arisen moral concerns which led to the anti-vivisection movement. In 1824, the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals1, one of the oldest animal welfare charities was formed. Later in 1876, an act for preventing cruelty to animals was made in the UK. In India, parallel movements were initiated in the year 1960. Then, the Animals Scientific Procedures Act (1986) came into existence and provided effective regulations enforced by law. During all these progressions, 3 Rs—replacement, reduction, and refinement of animals' use in research have been proposed. The idea of “replacement” has led researchers to search for alternatives. It mainly relied on replacing experimental mammals like rabbits, rats, and pigs with non-mammalian systems. Invertebrate models and micro-organisms were also introduced as a replacement for vertebrate models. Most of the intriguing biological questions could be addressed using a lower group of organisms. 
Invertebrates have made significant contributions in biomedical research as most of their organs and their physiology are analogous to mammals. Biomedical research using invertebrates has appeared in the scientific literature since the 1900s. They range from terrestrial invertebrates to freshwater and marine beings, including crustaceans and mollusks. During the last decade, articles published in PubMed revealed more than 250,000 entries on invertebrate models, which is comparatively higher than the previous year's reports (177,000). This indicates the efficiency of invertebrates as models in biomedical research. Significant discoveries were made using invertebrates ranging from embryonic development to aging. For example, Caenorhabditis elegans, a nematode, possesses several advantages over the vertebrate model for biomedical research. prompt: What are three different materials that were used to make breastplates in ancient times?
response_a:
1. Bronze: Breastplates made of bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, were commonly worn by ancient Greek and Roman soldiers as well as by some warriors in the Near East. The famous Achilles' shield from Homer's Iliad was also made of bronze and could be strapped onto his chest like a breastplate.

2. Leather: In ancient Egypt, breastplates made of thick leather were worn by charioteers and archers. These breastplates provided protection against arrows and other projectiles.

3. Plate armor: During the medieval period, European knights wore breastplates made of iron or steel plates that were attached to a leather or fabric backing. This type of armor offered greater protection than earlier materials and helped to establish the heavily armored knight as a dominant force on the battlefield.
response_b:
1. Bronze: In ancient Greece and Rome, breastplates were often made of bronze, which is an alloy of copper, tin, and sometimes other metals like zinc or nickel. The Greeks called this type of armor thorax, while the Romans referred to it as lorica hamata.

2. Leather: Less common but still used in some ancient civilizations was leather. In medieval Europe, for example, leather breastplates known as brigandines were popular among knights. These breastplates were lined with quilted fabric to provide extra protection.

3. Lamellar: Another ancient material used to create breastplates was lamellar. This type of armor consisted of small rectangular plates of metal (such as iron) that were attached to a backing material such as leather or cloth. The plates overlapped each other in a pattern, providing excellent coverage and flexibility. This type of armor was commonly used by ancient Persians and Turks.
